hero.headline: Speaker Johnson says Trump anti-weaponization fund off the table after pushback
hero.body:
Speaker Mike Johnson told President Trump that the proposed $1.776 billion anti-weaponization fund has become a political liability for Republicans trying to pass legislation in Congress, and indicated the administration is moving away from the proposal.

"I told him that it was a difficult prospect right now, given our vote tallies," Johnson said Tuesday, referring to Republicans' slim House majority. With narrow margins, Johnson explained, the ongoing controversy over the settlement fund threatens to divide his caucus and undermine efforts to advance other priorities.

The fund would compensate people who claim they were wrongfully prosecuted or targeted by the federal government. Since its announcement last month as part of a settlement in Trump's lawsuit against the IRS, the program has faced intense legal and political opposition.

A federal judge temporarily blocked the administration from transferring money from the fund after a lawsuit was filed to dissolve it. The court action combined with mounting Republican concern has pushed administration officials to back away from the proposal. The Justice Department said it would comply with the court order halting the fund's operations.

Republican criticism of the fund has been substantial. Vice President Mike Pence called the possibility of compensating January 6 rioters "deeply offensive," noting the concern is broadly shared among Republicans and Americans. Several states, including California, Illinois, New York and Connecticut, have proposed or announced plans to tax any distributions from the fund.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune suggested the best approach would be for the administration to voluntarily shut down the fund, saying "I do think the best way to handle it is if the administration decides to shut it down themselves."

Democrats have also mounted aggressive opposition to the program. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called it "corruption in broad daylight" and a "$1.8 billion Maga slush fund." Democrats have vowed to force Republicans to vote on measures blocking fund payments and preserving records related to the settlement.

Despite the apparent retreat by the Trump administration and Johnson's declaration that the fund is off the table, some Republicans are pushing for formal congressional action. Representative Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania said he plans to force a House vote on legislation to block the fund, suggesting lawmakers want an explicit legislative decision on the matter regardless of the administration's current position.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche was scheduled to testify before a House Appropriations Committee panel about Justice Department oversight, with the anti-weaponization fund expected to be a central topic of discussion. The fund's uncertain status reflects broader tensions between executive branch actions and congressional oversight authority, particularly given Republicans' narrow majority in the House.

cards.headline: Trump and Rubio say talks with Iran continue despite Tehran reports
cards.teaser: The White House said negotiations with Iran remain ongoing after Iranian media reported talks had stopped.
cards.body:
President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have stated that negotiations with Iran are ongoing, contradicting Iranian announcements that talks have ended. Trump told CNBC that reports of halted U.S.-Iran communications were false.

Iran's announcement came after disagreements over Israeli military operations in Lebanon and Gaza. Rubio told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that Iran has agreed to discuss nuclear program aspects it previously refused to negotiate, claiming a deal is within reach. Meanwhile, Tehran announced it was halting peace talks and moving to fully close the Strait of Hormuz.

cards.headline: Russia strikes Kyiv after week of threats against Ukraine
cards.teaser: Moscow launched deadly attacks on the Ukrainian capital following repeated warnings of a major strike.
cards.body:
Russia launched a massive overnight attack on Ukraine using 73 missiles and 656 drones, targeting five cities including Kyiv, Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Poltava, and Kharkiv. The strikes killed at least 18 people and injured dozens more, with some trapped under collapsed buildings. The assault included eight hypersonic Tsirkon missiles.

Following the attack, President Zelenskyy requested that Donald Trump send Patriot missiles to Ukraine. The strikes represent an escalation in Russia's assault on Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure across the country.

cards.headline: Israel strikes southern Lebanon as partial Hezbollah truce holds
cards.teaser: Israel continues military operations in southern Lebanon but has not targeted Beirut since a limited agreement was announced.
cards.body:
Israel has continued military strikes in southern Lebanon while maintaining a partial truce with Hezbollah that has prevented attacks on Beirut. The limited agreement, announced by the US, has effectively created geographical boundaries for the conflict rather than a comprehensive ceasefire.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stated that Israel would persist with its campaign against Hezbollah, even as Lebanese and Israeli officials held peace talks in Washington. The ongoing strikes demonstrate that the partial truce applies to specific areas while military operations continue elsewhere in southern Lebanon.

cards.headline: Trump confronted Netanyahu over threatened Beirut bombing resumption
cards.teaser: President Trump shouted at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a phone call about resuming strikes on Beirut.
cards.body:
President Trump angrily confronted Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over threats to resume airstrikes on Beirut's southern suburbs during a phone call on Monday. According to Axios, Trump shouted expletives at Netanyahu during the conversation, which took place after Iran said it would suspend talks with the US over Israel's Lebanon campaign.

The confrontation resulted in a halt to Israeli strikes on the Lebanese capital. Netanyahu subsequently faced criticism following Trump's intervention to stop the Beirut bombing campaign as Israel maintained a partial truce with Hezbollah.

cards.headline: Shipping Vessel Struck by Projectiles in Iraqi Port Amid Hormuz Negotiations
cards.body:
A container ship owned by Mediterranean Shipping Company was struck by two projectiles while docked at an Iraqi port, according to reports. The attack comes as the United States and Iran are engaged in negotiations to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for global oil shipments.

The incident highlights ongoing security risks for commercial shipping in the region despite diplomatic efforts. The Strait of Hormuz, which connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, serves as a transit point for roughly one-fifth of global oil supply. Its closure or disruption has significant implications for energy markets and international trade.

Mediterranean Shipping Company, one of the world's largest container shipping lines, operates hundreds of vessels worldwide. The company has not released details about the extent of damage to the vessel or whether any crew members were injured in the attack.

The timing of the attack underscores the fragile security situation in the Persian Gulf region even as diplomatic channels remain active. US-Iran talks have aimed to ease tensions and restore commercial shipping access through the strait, which Iran has threatened to block in past confrontations. The negotiations have been cited by market analysts as a factor in recent stock market gains, with investors viewing progress as a positive signal for global trade stability.

The attack on the MSC vessel demonstrates that threats to maritime commerce persist despite ongoing diplomatic engagement. Iraq's southern ports, including Umm Qasr and the oil terminal at Basra, handle significant volumes of containerized cargo and petroleum exports. Any escalation in attacks on commercial vessels could complicate negotiation efforts and raise insurance costs for shipping companies operating in the region.

cards.headline: Trump names housing official Bill Pulte as acting director of national intelligence
cards.body:
President Trump has appointed Bill Pulte, head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, to serve as acting director of national intelligence, replacing Tulsi Gabbard who recently announced her departure from the role.

Pulte, an heir to a home construction company fortune with no background in national security or intelligence, will assume the position immediately as acting director while continuing to lead the FHFA, which oversees the federal mortgage lenders Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Trump announced the decision on his Truth Social platform, stating that "William has deep experience managing the most sensitive matters in America."

The appointment has drawn immediate scrutiny from multiple quarters. Pulte's tenure at the housing agency has been marked by aggressive actions against targets he has publicly accused of wrongdoing. Shortly after arriving at the FHFA, he removed substantial portions of the boards overseeing Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and appointed himself as chair. Most notably, he has made extraordinary allegations against Trump's political opponents, including Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook, whom he has accused of mortgage fraud. Cook has denied any wrongdoing.

Senate Republican leaders have expressed considerable unease with the selection. Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters that the country does not need "a weaponized" director of national intelligence and warned that Pulte would face "a lengthy road ahead of him" if nominated for permanent confirmation. Thune emphasized the need for "professionals" in intelligence leadership rather than individuals who might pursue political opponents.

A former high-ranking official described Pulte's handling of the Cook case as "very bizarre." The growing questions surrounding his fraud referrals at the FHFA have raised concerns about whether similar patterns could extend to his intelligence role.

Critics have also pointed to Pulte's family background, with some describing him as a "nepo baby" given his ties to the PulteGroup building firm. However, the New York Times reported that Pulte no longer holds any official connection to the company after being pushed off the board in 2020. The Pulte Family Charitable Foundation, which has assets of approximately 500 million dollars, has taken steps to distance itself from him, stating in 2023 that "Bill Pulte is not a representative of, nor has he served in any capacity" for the foundation.

The appointment comes days after Gabbard's exit from the intelligence director position. According to sources briefed on internal discussions, Trump had been asking cabinet members as early as April whether he should replace Gabbard, who appeared marginalized during her tenure as Trump pursued aggressive foreign policy actions.

For Pulte to serve permanently in the role, the Senate must confirm his nomination, a process that will likely involve hearings and extensive questioning about his qualifications and potential conflicts of interest.

hero.headline: Two killed in Kenya protests against planned US Ebola quarantine center
hero.body:
Two people were shot dead during protests in Kenya against a United States plan to build an Ebola quarantine and treatment facility in the country. The demonstrations took place near the site of the proposed center, reflecting widespread public opposition to the project.

The Trump administration confirmed it was establishing a quarantine and treatment facility in Kenya for Americans exposed to or infected with Ebola. According to a White House official, the facility would provide high-quality care for Americans who need to quickly leave the Democratic Republic of the Congo without the risks of a lengthy transport back to the US. The center would also treat Americans who contract the virus, including critical care services, though cases would be evaluated for further transport to maximize patient outcomes.

The proposal has generated significant anger among Kenyan residents living near the proposed site at Laikipia Air Base in Nanyuki, about 120 miles from Nairobi. Local residents have organized demonstrations to oppose the facility, citing concerns that it could expose them to the virus in a country with no known Ebola cases.

Charles Mathenge, a taxi driver living near the proposed site, expressed the community's concerns. "Everybody should be quarantined in their home country. We shouldn't allow foreigners to bring us diseases," he said. "Kenya is our country, and we should be careful with it."

The plan has also drawn criticism from American public health experts. Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiologist and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University School of Public Health, raised ethical concerns about the approach. "There are profound ethical concerns with this approach," Nuzzo said. She warned that without adequate plans for safe quarantine of exposed individuals, the facilities could amplify virus spread and discourage people from disclosing exposure.

Jeremy Konyndyk, president of Refugees International and a former leader in the 2014-2015 Ebola response, expressed concern that the policy would discourage American health workers from volunteering. He noted that in 2014, the US avoided travel bans because such restrictions would ultimately be counterproductive to ending the outbreak. "It disincentivizes people from going," Konyndyk said of the current plan.

US officials did not clarify whether Americans would be allowed to return to the US if they chose not to go to Kenya, or whether further transport from the Kenya facility would be to the US or Europe. The US has banned green card holders and other recent travelers from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda, and South Sudan from entering the country.

The shooting deaths represent a serious escalation in public resistance to the proposed medical infrastructure. The violence is likely to intensify the debate over the facility and complicate US public health planning in the region.

cards.headline: British couple loses appeal of Iran jail sentence
cards.teaser: Lindsay and Craig Foreman were arrested during a global motorcycle journey and will remain imprisoned in Iran.
cards.body:
A British couple has lost their appeal against jail sentences in Iran, according to their family. Lindsay and Craig Foreman were arrested in January 2025 while traveling through Iran as part of a global motorcycle journey.

The unsuccessful appeal means the couple will continue serving their sentences in Iranian custody. The British government has not publicly commented on diplomatic efforts to secure their release.

cards.headline: Denmark's Frederiksen set for third term after Greenland stance
cards.teaser: The Danish prime minister will form a new government following months of negotiations, with her position on Greenland proving decisive.
cards.body:
Mette Frederiksen will begin a third consecutive term as Denmark's prime minister after securing a coalition agreement. The Social Democrat leader has formed a four-party, left-leaning minority government alongside the Social Liberals, the Green Left, and the centrist Moderates.

The coalition deal came after two months of negotiations following March elections in which 12 parties won parliamentary seats. Frederiksen's firm stance on Greenland helped secure the political support needed to form the new administration. The government is preparing to formally present its political programme.

cards.headline: Missing New Jersey congressman receives Trump endorsement before election
cards.teaser: Republican Tom Kean Jr. has not been seen for months but is expected to win his election despite his mysterious absence.
cards.body: Republican Congressman Tom Kean Jr. received an endorsement from Donald Trump ahead of Tuesday's election, despite not having been seen publicly for months. The New Jersey representative is still expected to win his race.

cards.headline: Trump calls Canada 51st state before trade talks
cards.teaser: The former president repeated his suggestion about Canadian statehood hours before a meeting between trade officials.
cards.body:
Donald Trump called Canada the 51st state shortly before scheduled trade negotiations in Washington. Canada's trade minister was in the US capital to meet with the US Trade Representative.

The remark came as the two countries discussed renewing the USMCA trade deal. Canada's trade minister had formally requested that the three North American nations renew their free trade pact in communications with his counterparts.

cards.headline: White House Correspondents' Dinner rescheduled for July 24 after shooting
cards.teaser: The annual White House Correspondents' Dinner will take place in July after a shooting disrupted the original event.
cards.body:
The White House Correspondents' Association rescheduled its annual dinner for July 24 after a shooting incident on April 25 forced the cancellation of the spring event. President Trump was swiftly evacuated from the gala following the incident.

Trump has confirmed he will attend the rescheduled July event, pledging his presence at the dinner that traditionally brings together journalists, government officials, and celebrities.

cards.headline: Trump signs order seeking voluntary AI safety testing
cards.teaser: President Trump signed an executive order asking AI companies to voluntarily submit new models for government testing before public release.
cards.body:
President Trump signed an executive order establishing a voluntary framework for AI safety review. Under the new guidelines, tech companies are asked to submit their most powerful models to the federal government for testing up to 30 days before public release.

The order aims to address national security and cybersecurity concerns related to artificial intelligence. However, the voluntary nature of the framework means tech companies are not required to comply. This approach reflects the administration's preference for industry cooperation over binding regulations, despite a shift toward more cautious AI oversight compared to earlier deregulatory positions.

cards.headline: Primary elections underway in California and other states
cards.teaser: Voters head to the polls in multiple state primary elections, including competitive races for California governor and Los Angeles mayor.
cards.body:
Primary elections are taking place in several states, with CNN reporting on competitive races for California governor and Los Angeles mayor. Republicans are seeking breakthroughs in multiple state contests, according to Fox News coverage of the primaries.

Politico identified five key storylines to follow as voting proceeds. Axios reported that the primaries feature Democratic Party divisions over the party's future direction. The Washington Post published analysis of the most significant races to monitor as results come in from polling locations across the participating states.

cards.headline: Israel strikes southern Lebanon as partial Hezbollah truce holds
cards.teaser: Israeli forces continued military operations in southern Lebanon while maintaining a halt to strikes on Beirut under a partial truce.
cards.body:
Israel has continued military operations in southern Lebanon while maintaining restraint in Beirut following a US-brokered agreement. The partial truce with Hezbollah has held in the capital, where Israel has refrained from strikes since the deal took effect.

The arrangement reflects the geographic scope of the ceasefire agreement, with fighting persisting in the south even as the capital remains largely untouched by Israeli military action under the terms of the partial cessation of hostilities.

cards.headline: Six States Sue Trump Administration Over Wind Farm Cancellation Deal
cards.teaser: Multiple states filed legal action challenging a federal agreement that paid a French energy company to terminate an offshore wind project.
cards.body:
Six state attorneys general filed a lawsuit Tuesday challenging the Trump administration's decision to cancel a major offshore wind lease off the coast of New York. In March, federal officials announced they would pay nearly $1 billion in taxpayer dollars to French energy company TotalEnergies to terminate the company's plans for two offshore wind farms off New York and North Carolina.

Under the agreement, TotalEnergies agreed to kill the wind projects and pledged not to develop any new offshore wind facilities in the United States. In exchange, the company committed to investing hundreds of millions of dollars in oil and gas projects. The states argue the cancellation deal is unlawful.

cards.headline: Trump Proposes Blocking Federal Grants That Conflict With Administration Priorities
cards.teaser: A new proposal would give the administration authority to deny federal grant funding to organizations that do not align with stated policy goals.
cards.body:
The Trump administration introduced a proposal that would allow it to block federal grants if recipients do not satisfy the administration's agenda or support what officials describe as anti-American values. The measure would give the executive branch expanded control over federal funding decisions.

The proposal applies to discretionary grant programs administered by federal agencies. It would establish criteria tied to administration policy priorities as a condition for receiving federal funds. The scope of affected grant programs and the specific definition of qualifying criteria have not been detailed in available reporting.

cards.headline: Stephen Curry Signs Endorsement Deal With Chinese Sneaker Company Li-Ning
cards.teaser: The NBA star reached an agreement with the Chinese athletic brand that includes plans for sportswear products and retail stores in both countries.
cards.body:
Stephen Curry signed an endorsement deal with Li-Ning, a Chinese sneaker and sportswear company. The agreement marks the largest partnership between an NBA star and a Chinese brand, according to reports.

The deal includes plans to develop sportswear and athleisure products under Curry's name. Li-Ning and Curry also plan to open retail stores across the United States and China as part of the partnership. The arrangement represents a significant expansion of commercial ties between American basketball stars and Chinese athletic wear manufacturers.

cards.headline: Stock Indexes Close Higher as Tech Stocks Advance
cards.teaser: Major US stock indexes ended the trading session with gains, driven by technology company shares.
cards.body:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average and other major indexes posted gains in trading, with technology stocks providing much of the upward momentum. Nvidia shares surged during the session, contributing to the tech sector's strength.

Alphabet shares declined despite broader market gains. Analysts cited optimism about US-Iran negotiations and continued investor interest in artificial intelligence companies as factors supporting market sentiment. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq also closed higher, with multiple indexes reaching record levels according to some reports.

cards.headline: Trump Megadonor Transferred $5.5 Million Estate to Anti-Vaccine Organization
cards.teaser: A member of the Mellon family gave adjacent Connecticut properties to Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s Children's Health Defense at no cost.
cards.body:
A Trump campaign megadonor from the Mellon family transferred Connecticut properties valued at $5.5 million to Children's Health Defense, the organization led by Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The gift consisted of adjacent properties covering approximately 300 acres and was completed at no cost to the recipient.

Children's Health Defense has been a prominent voice opposing childhood vaccination requirements and COVID-19 vaccine policies. Kennedy, who leads the organization, currently serves as Secretary of Health and Human Services in the Trump administration.

cards.headline: White House Correspondents Dinner Rescheduled for July
cards.teaser: The annual event will take place in July after being cut short in April when a gunman disrupted the proceedings.
cards.body:
The White House Correspondents Association has rescheduled its annual dinner for July 24 after the April event was cut short by a shooting. President Trump, who was evacuated from the gala following the incident on April 25, confirmed he will attend the rescheduled event.

The dinner traditionally brings together journalists, government officials, and celebrities. The association is preparing security measures for the summer gathering.

hero.headline: Ebola outbreak shrinks as testing reveals hundreds of suspected cases negative
hero.body:
Ebola outbreak in Congo hampered by conflict and medical shortages

An Ebola outbreak in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo is spreading faster than the response can contain it, according to the head of the World Health Organization. The situation has been worsened by armed conflict in the region and critical shortages of medical supplies.

As of Tuesday, Congo's health ministry confirmed 101 Ebola cases, though the number of suspected cases is approaching 1,000. At least 220 suspected deaths have been reported. The outbreak was confirmed on May 15 in Ituri province, which borders South Sudan and Uganda. It has since spread to rebel-held areas of North Kivu and South Kivu provinces.

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for an immediate ceasefire in eastern Congo to help control the outbreak. He described the situation as a "catastrophic collision of disease and conflict" and said he would travel to the DRC this week. Tedros emphasized that stopping transmission depends on humanitarian access, but ongoing armed clashes are displacing populations and making it impossible to track cases and their contacts.

The conflict is directly hampering medical response efforts. Health facilities have been attacked by people demanding the release of Ebola victims' bodies for traditional burials, which involve family members washing and touching the deceased. Since Ebola victims' bodies remain highly contagious, these practices have spread the disease in previous outbreaks. During attacks on a hospital in Mongbwalu on Saturday and Sunday, 25 Ebola patients fled after unidentified individuals burned isolation tents.

Medical staff are also facing severe equipment shortages. A doctor in Butembo reported having only two body bags remaining and said the facility lacks adequate soap, chlorine, and personal protective gear including boots, body suits, masks, and gloves. The doctor noted that foreign aid cuts to international and local aid organizations have contributed to these shortages.

Save the Children reported that a quarter of confirmed deaths have been children. The organization called for infection prevention measures to be urgently scaled up, noting that years of conflict have weakened community systems and left many young people malnourished and vulnerable to the virus.

Uganda has reported seven confirmed Ebola cases and one death. In response, Uganda closed its border with the DRC for four weeks, with exceptions only for Ebola response teams, humanitarian operations, security operations, and food and cargo transport. Any authorized traveler from the Congo must undergo mandatory self-isolation for 21 days.

Aid groups are rushing staff and equipment to eastern Congo, but community distrust has led to attacks on health workers, further hampering containment efforts. The UN refugee agency reported that transit and reception sites in Uganda's West Nile region are operating at more than double capacity.

cards.headline: Amazon faces class action lawsuit over Ring facial recognition storage
cards.teaser: A Virginia resident filed a class action lawsuit in Seattle claiming Ring stores facial images of people without their consent.
cards.body:
Amazon faces a class action lawsuit over its Ring doorbell camera system and its Familiar Faces feature. Virginia resident Charles Sigwalt filed the lawsuit in Seattle, challenging whether Amazon has the legal right to collect and store biometric data of individuals who pass by homes equipped with Ring devices.

The Familiar Faces feature uses facial recognition technology to identify people captured by Ring cameras. Sigwalt alleges the feature stores images of passersby without obtaining their consent, including people who have no relationship with the device owner.

cards.headline: Google adds AI deepfake detection to Android phones to fight scam calls
cards.teaser: Android phones will detect spoofed calls and AI voice impersonation as scammers increasingly mimic trusted contacts.
cards.body:
Google has introduced fake call detection technology for Android devices to combat AI-powered scam calls. The feature identifies when callers spoof trusted phone numbers to appear as legitimate contacts and detects AI-generated voices designed to impersonate real people. The technology addresses a shift in scam tactics as criminals increasingly target people who refuse to answer calls from unknown numbers.

The detection system was included in Google's latest Android update alongside other features like expanded Quick Share compatibility for AirDrop devices and new AI tools for Play Books.

cards.headline: Fusion startup Focused Energy raises $240 million for laser-powered reactor
cards.teaser: The company secured one of the largest Series A rounds in fusion energy to develop laser-based fusion technology.
cards.body:
Focused Energy raised $240 million in Series A funding to advance its laser-powered fusion technology. The round ranks among the largest early-stage investments in the fusion sector.

The startup is part of a competitive landscape where multiple companies are developing fusion energy with different technical approaches. Focused Energy's laser-based method for triggering fusion reactions distinguishes it from competitors using magnetic confinement technology.

cards.headline: Microsoft launches Scout AI assistant for Microsoft 365 users
cards.teaser: The company introduced Scout at its Build conference as an AI assistant built on OpenClaw technology.
cards.body:
Microsoft has introduced Scout, a new AI assistant built on OpenClaw technology for Microsoft 365 users. Unveiled at the Build developer conference, Scout integrates directly into Microsoft 365 applications including Outlook, OneDrive, and Microsoft Teams.

The always-on assistant is designed to help employees with routine tasks such as organizing calendars, drafting emails, managing expense reports, and other productivity functions. By embedding AI capabilities into familiar workplace tools, Scout brings OpenClaw's power and flexibility into Microsoft's existing productivity ecosystem.

cards.headline: Former Anduril engineer raises $42 million for composite parts manufacturing
cards.teaser: Layup Parts secured funding to streamline composite materials production with faster and cheaper manufacturing methods.
cards.body:
Layup Parts co-founder Zack Eakin raised $42 million to transform composite parts manufacturing. Drawing on his motorsports background and experience at defense and aerospace companies—including Anduril and roles working for Palmer Luckey and Elon Musk—Eakin identified inefficiencies in how composites are produced.

The company positions itself as a streamlined alternative for manufacturers across aerospace, automotive, and other industries that rely on composite materials. Eakin's goal is to make composites faster, cheaper, and more accessible for production.

cards.headline: Reading startup Everand bundles ebooks, audiobooks, and book clubs
cards.teaser: The subscription service combines digital reading materials with Fable's book club community to compete with Amazon.
cards.body:
Everand has launched a subscription service combining ebooks, audiobooks, and book club features into a single platform. The service integrates Fable's book club community, allowing subscribers to access both content formats alongside social reading features.

This bundled approach positions Everand as a competitor to Amazon's separate Kindle and Audible services. By merging multiple reading formats with community discussion tools, the startup aims to differentiate itself in the digital reading market.

hero.headline: Browns trade Myles Garrett to Rams for Jared Verse and three draft picks
hero.body:
The Cleveland Browns traded star edge rusher Myles Garrett to the Los Angeles Rams on Monday in exchange for linebacker Jared Verse and three draft picks. The deal marks a significant shift for both franchises as they reshape their rosters.

Garrett, 30, is a two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year and seven-time Pro Bowl selection. Since the Browns selected him first overall in 2017, he has become one of the league's most dominant defensive players. He holds the record for most sacks (125.5), pressures (413), and tackles for loss (149) among all players since his draft year. In 2025, he set a single-season sacks record with 23.

The star edge rusher had requested a trade from the Browns in 2024 after the team finished with a 3-14 record, stating he wanted to play for a championship contender. However, the Browns signed him to a four-year extension worth 160 million dollars the following month, making him the highest-paid non-quarterback in league history at that time. Despite his individual success, the Browns finished the 2025 season with a 5-12 record and missed the playoffs for the second consecutive year.

The trade became possible after the Browns and Garrett agreed to modify his contract in March, deferring option payments across the 2026-28 seasons. Browns general manager Andrew Berry explained the decision, saying the team faced "a legitimate crossroads: do we hold on to a truly generational player who has become the identity of our team, or do we make the difficult decision that we think is best for the organization over the long run?"

The Rams received a 2027 first-round selection, a 2028 second-round pick, and a 2029 third-round selection as part of the trade. Verse, 25, was a first-round draft pick by the Rams in 2024 and earned Defensive Rookie of the Year honors. He was selected to the Pro Bowl this past season and has recorded 12 career sacks along with 22 tackles for loss.

For Los Angeles, the trade represents an aggressive move to compete after losing to the Seattle Seahawks in last season's NFC Championship Game. The Rams have a history of making bold roster moves, most notably trading for quarterback Matthew Stafford in 2021, who led them to a Super Bowl victory in his first season. Stafford won his first NFL MVP award last season.

Garrett's arrival in Los Angeles marks the first time the reigning AP NFL MVP and Defensive Player of the Year will be teammates. The Rams will host Super Bowl LXI at SoFi Stadium next February, giving them the opportunity to pursue another championship on their home field.

cards.headline: Seahawks extend pass rusher Derick Hall with three-year, $42 million deal
cards.teaser: Seattle has signed defensive player Derick Hall to a $42 million contract extension.
cards.body:
The Seattle Seahawks and pass rusher Derick Hall have agreed to a three-year contract extension worth $42 million. The deal secures Hall's services through the 2028 season and represents a significant investment in the team's defensive future.

Hall, a former Auburn standout, has emerged as a key contributor to Seattle's defense. The extension reflects the Seahawks' commitment to building their pass rush around young talent. The contract makes Hall one of the higher-paid players at his position in the league.

cards.headline: Stephen Curry signs shoe deal with Chinese company Li-Ning
cards.teaser: The NBA star has partnered with Chinese sportswear brand Li-Ning following his split from Under Armour.
cards.body:
Stephen Curry has signed a new shoe deal with Chinese sportswear company Li-Ning, months after ending his partnership with Under Armour. The agreement marks a major win for the Chinese brand as it seeks to expand its global presence in the athletic footwear market.

The deal brings one of basketball's biggest stars to a company looking to compete with established Western brands. Curry's move to Li-Ning represents a shift in the sneaker industry landscape, as Chinese companies increasingly sign high-profile athletes. The partnership gives Li-Ning access to Curry's substantial fan base and global recognition.

cards.headline: Odell Beckham Jr. returns to Giants on one-year minimum deal
cards.teaser: The receiver has signed with New York, returning to the team where he began his NFL career.
cards.body:
Odell Beckham Jr. has signed a one-year minimum contract with the New York Giants, returning to the franchise that drafted him. The Giants also signed receivers JuJu Smith-Schuster and Braxton Berrios to similar one-year minimum deals while releasing kicker Jason Sanders.

Beckham's return marks his second stint with the organization after establishing himself as one of the league's top receivers during his initial years in New York. The Giants are adding veteran experience to their receiving corps with the signings of Beckham, Smith-Schuster, and Berrios as they look to bolster their offensive options.

cards.headline: Lawmakers adjourn without passing Bears stadium bill
cards.teaser: Illinois legislators ended their session without approving funding for a Chicago Bears stadium.
cards.body:
Illinois lawmakers adjourned without passing legislation to provide public funding for a Chicago Bears stadium, leaving the team's long-term future in the state uncertain. Hammond's mayor expects the Bears to make a decision about their location by the end of June.

The failed bill creates questions about whether the Bears will remain in Illinois or pursue options elsewhere. Political leaders expressed differing reactions to the outcome, with some disappointed by the missed opportunity and others opposed to the use of public funds. The Bears now face a decision about their next steps, including whether to pursue the Halas family legacy in Illinois or explore alternatives.

cards.headline: FIFA introduces new offside technology for 2026 World Cup
cards.teaser: The delayed offside flag may become obsolete with new system for next summer's tournament.
cards.body:
FIFA has unveiled new offside detection technology set to debut at the 2026 World Cup. The system is designed to make the delayed offside flag nearly obsolete by providing faster and more accurate offside decisions during matches.

This technological advancement represents a significant shift in how soccer officiating handles one of the sport's most contentious calls. The 2026 World Cup will be the first tournament to implement this system.

cards.headline: Fulham manager Marco Silva leaving to join Benfica
cards.teaser: Silva will depart after five years managing the London club.
cards.body:
Marco Silva has left Fulham after five years as head coach. The 48-year-old Portuguese manager is closing in on a deal to take over at Benfica, where he will replace José Mourinho, who is heading to Real Madrid.

During his time at Fulham, Silva led the club to consecutive 11th-place Premier League finishes and a Carabao Cup semi-final in 2023-24. The team also achieved their record Premier League points tally of 54 this season, along with 15 wins, their best haul in a single Premier League campaign.

hero.headline: Martin Scorsese Joins AI Company as Adviser, Plans to Use Technology for Film Storyboarding
hero.body:
Director Martin Scorsese has joined artificial intelligence firm Black Forest Labs as an adviser and announced plans to use the technology in his filmmaking process. The Oscar-winning filmmaker said he intends to employ AI tools for storyboarding future movies.

Scorsese framed his decision as part of cinema's natural evolution. He noted that film is a relatively young medium at approximately 125 years old and said creators must remain open to how it can develop. The director positioned his involvement with Black Forest Labs as an effort to expand creative possibilities and deliver deeper experiences for audiences.

The announcement makes Scorsese the latest prominent Hollywood director to publicly embrace artificial intelligence technology for filmmaking purposes. His decision to work with an AI company represents a shift for the director, who has built his decades-long career using traditional filmmaking techniques. Scorsese's films, including Taxi Driver, Goodfellas, and The Irishman, have relied on conventional production methods throughout his time in the industry.

Black Forest Labs develops AI tools aimed at creative industries. The company has not specified which particular technologies Scorsese will use for storyboarding or how extensively AI will feature in his upcoming projects. Storyboarding traditionally involves hand-drawn or digitally created sequential images that map out a film's visual plan before shooting begins.

The move comes as artificial intelligence tools have gained traction across entertainment sectors, with studios and creators exploring applications ranging from script analysis to visual effects generation. Scorsese's participation as an adviser suggests he will help shape how the company's tools are developed for filmmakers. His involvement may influence how other established directors approach AI technology in their own work.

cards.headline: Netflix Communications Chief Emily Feingold Leaves After Eight Years
cards.teaser: Emily Feingold, who served as Netflix's VP of communications, has departed the streaming company.
cards.body:
Emily Feingold has left her position as vice president of communications at Netflix after eight years with the streaming service. She joined Netflix in 2017 as communications director before being promoted to the VP role in 2022.

Feingold was credited with helping raise Netflix's public profile and protecting the company's reputation during her tenure. The reason for her departure has not been disclosed by Netflix or Feingold.

cards.headline: Robert Pattinson Installed Home Gym for The Batman: Part II After Body Criticism
cards.teaser: The actor addressed criticism of his physique in the first Batman film and discussed preparations for the sequel.
cards.body:
Robert Pattinson told GQ magazine he installed a home gym to build muscle before filming The Batman: Part II. The actor was responding to viewers who criticized his physical appearance in the 2022 film The Batman.

Pattinson said he worked out every day in preparation for the sequel. He also revealed that The Batman: Part II includes 11 weeks of night shoots. The film is currently in production.

cards.headline: Rapper Quando Rondo Moved to Halfway House After 15 Months in Prison
cards.teaser: The Savannah rapper was released from prison to a halfway house following his guilty plea on a marijuana charge.
cards.body:
Quando Rondo has been released from prison to a halfway house after serving 15 months. The Savannah, Georgia rapper had been incarcerated following a guilty plea to a marijuana charge in 2024.

The move to a halfway house represents a step toward full release for the rising rapper. Halfway houses typically serve as transitional facilities where individuals complete the remainder of their sentences while reintegrating into the community.

cards.headline: Chrissie Hynde Asks Concertgoers to Stop Using Cellphones During Shows
cards.teaser: The Pretenders lead singer wrote to fans requesting they put away phones and focus on the performance.
cards.body:
Chrissie Hynde, lead singer of the Pretenders, has published a letter urging concertgoers to put away their cellphones during shows. She wants fans to experience performances directly rather than through their devices, without recording or viewing the concert through screens.

Hynde's message is part of a broader push by musicians against phone use at live events. Her blunt letter represents the latest example of artists expressing frustration with widespread device distraction in concert venues.

cards.headline: AAA Wrestling Mask Match Video Draws More Than 2 Million Views
cards.teaser: A mask versus mask match from the Noche de los Grandes event attracted a large online audience across two platforms.
cards.body:
The mask versus mask match featuring El Grande Americano at AAA's Noche de los Grandes event has accumulated over 2 million combined views across platforms. The WWE YouTube channel's official video of the event reached more than 1.8 million views, while AAA's full event video garnered over 436,000 views.

In lucha libre wrestling, mask versus mask matches represent a traditional high-stakes stipulation where the loser must unmask. The strong viewership numbers demonstrate significant audience interest in AAA's programming.

cards.headline: Morgan Wallen Jokes About Piano Incident After Denver Show
cards.teaser: The country singer addressed technical difficulties that led him to flip a piano during a recent Denver performance.
cards.body:
Morgan Wallen posted a message to fans assuring them his piano is functioning properly after he flipped the instrument at a Denver concert. The incident occurred when technical difficulties interrupted the show.

Wallen's response poked fun at the moment, which drew comparisons to Billy Joel's famous piano antics. The country star has been touring extensively and the Denver show was part of his current concert schedule.

hero.headline: Speaker Johnson says Trump anti-weaponization fund off the table after pushback
hero.body:
Speaker Mike Johnson told President Trump that the proposed $1.776 billion anti-weaponization fund has become a political liability for Republicans trying to pass legislation in Congress, and indicated the administration is moving away from the proposal.

"I told him that it was a difficult prospect right now, given our vote tallies," Johnson said Tuesday, referring to Republicans' slim House majority. With narrow margins, Johnson explained, the ongoing controversy over the settlement fund threatens to divide his caucus and undermine efforts to advance other priorities.

The fund would compensate people who claim they were wrongfully prosecuted or targeted by the federal government. Since its announcement last month as part of a settlement in Trump's lawsuit against the IRS, the program has faced intense legal and political opposition.

A federal judge temporarily blocked the administration from transferring money from the fund after a lawsuit was filed to dissolve it. The court action combined with mounting Republican concern has pushed administration officials to back away from the proposal. The Justice Department said it would comply with the court order halting the fund's operations.

Republican criticism of the fund has been substantial. Vice President Mike Pence called the possibility of compensating January 6 rioters "deeply offensive," noting the concern is broadly shared among Republicans and Americans. Several states, including California, Illinois, New York and Connecticut, have proposed or announced plans to tax any distributions from the fund.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune suggested the best approach would be for the administration to voluntarily shut down the fund, saying "I do think the best way to handle it is if the administration decides to shut it down themselves."

Democrats have also mounted aggressive opposition to the program. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called it "corruption in broad daylight" and a "$1.8 billion Maga slush fund." Democrats have vowed to force Republicans to vote on measures blocking fund payments and preserving records related to the settlement.

Despite the apparent retreat by the Trump administration and Johnson's declaration that the fund is off the table, some Republicans are pushing for formal congressional action. Representative Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania said he plans to force a House vote on legislation to block the fund, suggesting lawmakers want an explicit legislative decision on the matter regardless of the administration's current position.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche was scheduled to testify before a House Appropriations Committee panel about Justice Department oversight, with the anti-weaponization fund expected to be a central topic of discussion. The fund's uncertain status reflects broader tensions between executive branch actions and congressional oversight authority, particularly given Republicans' narrow majority in the House.

cards.headline: Acting Attorney General Blanche testifies before House on Justice Department oversight
cards.teaser: Todd Blanche appeared before House appropriators as questions mount over the administration's proposed compensation fund.
cards.body:
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche testified before a House Appropriations Committee panel on Tuesday regarding Justice Department oversight. The hearing addressed the Trump administration's proposed $1.776 billion compensation fund for individuals claiming wrongful prosecution.

The so-called anti-weaponization fund has sparked significant controversy. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) announced plans to force a House vote on legislation blocking the fund, despite the Department of Justice's position on the matter. The proposal has created challenges for Republican leadership attempting to advance related legislation.

cards.headline: California governor primary underway with crowded field
cards.teaser: Democrats Katie Porter, Tom Steyer and Xavier Becerra face Republicans Chad Bianco and Steve Hilton to replace Gavin Newsom.
cards.body:
California voters are casting ballots in a primary election to select nominees for governor. The race to replace Gov. Gavin Newsom features three Democrats and two Republicans competing for their party nominations.

Democrats Katie Porter, Tom Steyer and Xavier Becerra are seeking their party's nomination, while Republicans Chad Bianco and Steve Hilton are vying to advance to the general election. The next governor of deep-blue California will almost certainly be a Democrat. Xavier Becerra, the establishment favorite, represents a traditional approach to governance centered on corporate-friendly liberalism.

cards.headline: Appeals court dismisses youth lawsuit challenging Trump energy orders
cards.teaser: The Ninth Circuit ruled 22 young plaintiffs have no legal standing to sue over executive orders on federal energy policy.
cards.body:
A federal appeals court has dismissed a lawsuit filed by 22 young people challenging President Trump's executive orders on federal energy policy. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled that the plaintiffs lack legal standing to bring the case.

The panel determined that federal courts cannot grant the relief the young people sought, which included an injunction blocking the energy orders. The judges found that issuing such an injunction would improperly constrain executive authority beyond what courts are empowered to do.

cards.headline: Trump appoints housing finance director Bill Pulte as acting intelligence chief
cards.teaser: President Trump tapped the Federal Housing Finance Agency director to lead the nation's intelligence services.
cards.body:
President Trump has appointed Bill Pulte, head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, to serve as acting director of national intelligence. Pulte, heir to a home construction company fortune, takes the role days after Tulsi Gabbard's departure from the position.

The appointment has raised concerns among lawmakers and officials in Washington. Pulte has no national intelligence experience and limited government background before Trump appointed him to lead the FHFA, which oversees Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Since arriving at that agency, Pulte has made significant personnel changes, firing board members and appointing himself as chair.

cards.headline: US ambassador to Canada shares Trump post calling Canada 51st state
cards.teaser: Pete Hoekstra reposted the president's social media message renewing his push to acquire the northern neighbor.
cards.body:
U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra shared a post from President Trump about Canada becoming the 51st state. The ambassador amplified Trump's message on social media by posting a screenshot of a Truth Social post in which the president wrote "51st State!" and linked to a Bloomberg article.

The move drew attention to Trump's ongoing statements about acquiring Canada. Hoekstra's decision to amplify the president's message on social media was notable given his diplomatic position representing the United States to the Canadian government.

cards.headline: Pennsylvania Republican plans vote on bill blocking compensation fund
cards.teaser: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick said he will force a House vote despite Justice Department backing away from the proposal.
cards.body:
Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick announced plans to force a House vote on legislation that would block the Trump administration's proposed anti-weaponization fund. The nearly $1.8 billion fund would compensate individuals who claim they were unfairly targeted by the government.

Fitzpatrick's push for a vote comes after the Justice Department backed away from the proposal. Speaker Mike Johnson said the fund made it difficult for Republicans to advance other legislation, calling it "off the table."
